claim: Many plasmids encode antibiotic resistance genes.
source: Many plasmids encode antibiotic resistance genes.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about plasmids.

claim: Plasmids can be rapidly disseminated through conjugation.
source: Through conjugation, plasmids can be rapidly disseminated.
evidence: This is established knowledge about plasmid transfer mechanisms.

claim: Gut luminal donor/recipient blooms promote plasmid dissemination among Enterobacteriaceae.
source: Previous work identified gut luminal donor/recipient blooms and tissue-lodged plasmid-bearing persister cells of the enteric pathogen Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (S.Tm) that survive antibiotic therapy in host tissues, as factors promoting plasmid dissemination among Enterobacteriaceae.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Tissue-lodged plasmid-bearing persister cells of S.Tm that survive antibiotic therapy promote plasmid dissemination among Enterobacteriaceae.
source: Previous work identified gut luminal donor/recipient blooms and tissue-lodged plasmid-bearing persister cells of the enteric pathogen Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (S.Tm) that survive antibiotic therapy in host tissues, as factors promoting plasmid dissemination among Enterobacteriaceae.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The buildup of tissue reservoirs and their contribution to plasmid spread await experimental demonstration.
source: However, the buildup of tissue reservoirs and their contribution to plasmid spread await experimental demonstration.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: Re-seeding-plasmid acquisition-invasion cycles by S.Tm can serve to diversify tissue-lodged plasmid reservoirs.
source: Here, we asked if re-seeding-plasmid acquisition-invasion cycles by S.Tm could serve to diversify tissue-lodged plasmid reservoirs, and thereby promote plasmid spread.
evidence: This is the research question being investigated in the study.

claim: S.Tm cells re-seeding the gut lumen initiate clonal expansion.
source: Starting with intraperitoneal mouse infections, we demonstrate that S.Tm cells re-seeding the gut lumen initiate clonal expansion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: ESBL plasmid-encoded gut luminal antibiotic degradation by donors can foster recipient survival under beta-lactam antibiotic treatment.
source: Extended spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) plasmid-encoded gut luminal antibiotic degradation by donors can foster recipient survival under beta-lactam antibiotic treatment, enhancing transconjugant formation upon re-seeding.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: ESBL plasmid-encoded gut luminal antibiotic degradation enhances transconjugant formation upon re-seeding.
source: Extended spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) plasmid-encoded gut luminal antibiotic degradation by donors can foster recipient survival under beta-lactam antibiotic treatment, enhancing transconjugant formation upon re-seeding.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: S.Tm transconjugants can re-enter host tissues introducing the new plasmid into the tissue-lodged reservoir.
source: S.Tm transconjugants can subsequently re-enter host tissues introducing the new plasmid into the tissue-lodged reservoir.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Recipient migration into the gut lumen is rate-limiting for plasmid transfer dynamics in the experimental model.
source: Population dynamics analyses pinpoint recipient migration into the gut lumen as rate-limiting for plasmid transfer dynamics in our model.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling and analysis of experimental data.

claim: Priority effects may be a limiting factor for reservoir formation in host tissues.
source: Priority effects may be a limiting factor for reservoir formation in host tissues.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from the data.

claim: Luminal antibiotic degradation can promote the accumulation and spread of plasmids within a host over time.
source: Overall, our proof-of-principle data indicates that luminal antibiotic degradation and shuttling between the gut lumen and tissue-resident reservoirs can promote the accumulation and spread of plasmids within a host over time.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Shuttling between the gut lumen and tissue-resident reservoirs can promote the accumulation and spread of plasmids within a host over time.
source: Overall, our proof-of-principle data indicates that luminal antibiotic degradation and shuttling between the gut lumen and tissue-resident reservoirs can promote the accumulation and spread of plasmids within a host over time.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The accumulation of antibiotic resistance genes in pathogenic bacterial strains is an important cause of antibiotic treatment failure.
source: The accumulation of antibiotic resistance genes in pathogenic bacterial strains is an important cause of antibiotic treatment failure.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Conjugative antibiotic resistance plasmids are key drivers of the accumulation of antibiotic resistance genes.
source: Conjugative antibiotic resistance plasmids are key drivers of this accumulation, accelerating the emergence of new bacterial strains genetically resistant to antibiotics (Wright, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wright, 2007.

claim: Conjugative antibiotic resistance plasmids accelerate the emergence of new bacterial strains genetically resistant to antibiotics.
source: Conjugative antibiotic resistance plasmids are key drivers of this accumulation, accelerating the emergence of new bacterial strains genetically resistant to antibiotics (Wright, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wright, 2007.

claim: The mechanisms that contribute to the spread of resistance plasmids within an infected host are still not fully established.
source: The mechanisms that contribute to the spread of resistance plasmids within an infected host are still not fully established.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Plasmid spread within mammalian hosts can be aided by tissue-lodged reservoirs of bacterial cells phenotypically recalcitrant to antibiotic therapy.
source: Plasmid spread within such hosts can be aided by tissue-lodged reservoirs of bacterial cells phenotypically recalcitrant to antibiotic therapy (Bakkeren et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bakkeren et al., 2019.

claim: Persistence refers to a property of bacterial populations in which one subpopulation is killed by an antibiotic parallel to another subpopulation that is killed slowly ('persisters'), defined by phenotypic and not genotypic properties.
source: This process is called persistence and refers to a property of bacterial populations in which one subpopulation is killed by an antibiotic parallel to another subpopulation that is killed slowly ('persisters'), defined by phenotypic and not genotypic properties (Balaban et al., 2019; Gollan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to Balaban et al., 2019 and Gollan et al., 2019.

claim: Persisters can lead to antibiotic treatment failure.
source: Persisters can not only lead to antibiotic treatment failure, but they also have important implications for the evolution of antibiotic resistance (Levin-Reisman et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020; Windels et al., 2019) or virulence (Bakkeren et al., 2020; Diard et al., 2014), and serve as long-term reservoirs promoting the spread of resistance plasmids.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Persisters have important implications for the evolution of antibiotic resistance.
source: Persisters can not only lead to antibiotic treatment failure, but they also have important implications for the evolution of antibiotic resistance (Levin-Reisman et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020; Windels et al., 2019) or virulence (Bakkeren et al., 2020; Diard et al., 2014), and serve as long-term reservoirs promoting the spread of resistance plasmids.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Levin-Reisman et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020; Windels et al., 2019.

claim: Persisters have important implications for the evolution of virulence.
source: Persisters can not only lead to antibiotic treatment failure, but they also have important implications for the evolution of antibiotic resistance (Levin-Reisman et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020; Windels et al., 2019) or virulence (Bakkeren et al., 2020; Diard et al., 2014), and serve as long-term reservoirs promoting the spread of resistance plasmids.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bakkeren et al., 2020; Diard et al., 2014.

claim: Persisters serve as long-term reservoirs promoting the spread of resistance plasmids.
source: Persisters can not only lead to antibiotic treatment failure, but they also have important implications for the evolution of antibiotic resistance (Levin-Reisman et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020; Windels et al., 2019) or virulence (Bakkeren et al., 2020; Diard et al., 2014), and serve as long-term reservoirs promoting the spread of resistance plasmids.
evidence: This is a claim supported by the authors' previous work.

claim: Invasive S.Tm cells form reservoirs of recalcitrant cells inside of host tissues that are difficult to treat with antibiotics.
source: Invasive S.Tm cells form reservoirs of recalcitrant cells inside of host tissues (i.e. tissue persister reservoirs) that are difficult to treat with antibiotics (Bakkeren et al., 2019; Claudi et al., 2014; Diard et al., 2014; Helaine et al., 2014; Kaiser et al., 2014; Stapels et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: After antibiotic treatment, S.Tm cells can re-seed the gut lumen from their tissue reservoirs along with any plasmids they carry.
source: After treatment, these S.Tm cells can re-seed the gut lumen from their reservoirs along with any plasmids they carry.
evidence: This is a claim based on previous work and the current study.

claim: Re-seeding from tissue reservoirs provides plasmids with the opportunity to conjugate into new bacteria in the gut lumen.
source: In the gut lumen, this re-seeding provides the plasmids with the opportunity to conjugate into new bacteria.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental setup and results.

claim: Plasmids can subvert persisters to ensure long-term association within a given host.
source: Thereby, plasmids can subvert persisters to ensure long-term association within a given host.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and previous work.

claim: S.Tm tissue invasion creates an antibiotic susceptible subpopulation within the host tissues.
source: Besides persisters, S.Tm tissue invasion also creates an antibiotic susceptible subpopulation within the host tissues.
evidence: This is established knowledge about S.Tm infection.

claim: In the absence of antibiotic therapy, antibiotic susceptible cells in tissue reservoirs are generally more numerous than the persisters.
source: In the absence of antibiotic therapy, the latter cells are generally more numerous than the persisters and are thought to drive chronic infections (Claudi et al., 2014; Kaiser et al., 2014; Lawley et al., 2008; Monack et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Claudi et al., 2014; Kaiser et al., 2014; Lawley et al., 2008; Monack et al., 2004.

claim: Antibiotic susceptible cells in tissue reservoirs are thought to drive chronic infections.
source: In the absence of antibiotic therapy, the latter cells are generally more numerous than the persisters and are thought to drive chronic infections (Claudi et al., 2014; Kaiser et al., 2014; Lawley et al., 2008; Monack et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Claudi et al., 2014; Kaiser et al., 2014; Lawley et al., 2008; Monack et al., 2004.

claim: Cells that constitute tissue reservoirs during chronic infection are known to re-seed the gut lumen over time.
source: Moreover, cells that constitute tissue reservoirs during chronic infection are known to re-seed the gut lumen over time (Lam and Monack, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lam and Monack, 2014.

claim: The role of the non-persister, tissue-lodged pathogen population in plasmid dissemination remained to be formally established prior to this study.
source: However, the role of this second, non-persister, tissue-lodged pathogen population in plasmid dissemination remained to be formally established.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: Antibiotic persistence is defined by biphasic killing curves defining the susceptible and tolerant subpopulations.
source: Although very specific characteristics define antibiotic persistence (i.e. biphasic killing curves defining the susceptible and tolerant subpopulations) (Balaban et al., 2019), there are many similarities to persistent (aka long-term, chronic) infection.
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to Balaban et al., 2019.

claim: There are many similarities between antibiotic persistence and persistent (long-term, chronic) infection.
source: Although very specific characteristics define antibiotic persistence (i.e. biphasic killing curves defining the susceptible and tolerant subpopulations) (Balaban et al., 2019), there are many similarities to persistent (aka long-term, chronic) infection.
evidence: This is a statement based on knowledge and inference.

claim: Numerous bacterial pathogens can survive or evade host immune defenses and antibiotics alike in a recalcitrant state.
source: Numerous bacterial pathogens can survive or evade host immune defenses and antibiotics alike in a recalcitrant state (e.g. Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, or Salmonella enterica) (Bakkeren et al., 2020; Gollan et al., 2019; Grant and Hung, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bakkeren et al., 2020; Gollan et al., 2019; Grant and Hung, 2013.

claim: Tissue reservoirs of S.Tm antibiotic persisters located in the intestinal mucosa or systemic sites can re-seed the gut lumen after the cessation of antibiotic therapy in mouse models.
source: Using mouse models, tissue reservoirs of S.Tm antibiotic persisters located in the intestinal mucosa or systemic sites can re-seed the gut lumen after the cessation of antibiotic therapy (Bakkeren et al., 2019; Diard et al., 2014; Endt et al., 2012; Kaiser et al., 2014; Onwuezobe et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bakkeren et al., 2019; Diard et al., 2014; Endt et al., 2012; Kaiser et al., 2014; Onwuezobe et al., 2012.

claim: In chronically infected hosts, the pathogen population tends to diversify forming non-growing and growing subpopulations which are kept in check by immune defenses.
source: In chronically infected hosts, the pathogen population tends to diversify forming non-growing and growing subpopulations which are kept in check by immune defenses, but can rise upon neutralization of cytokines (e.g. IFNγ or TNFα) (Monack et al., 2004; Pham et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Monack et al., 2004; Pham et al., 2020.

claim: Pathogen subpopulations in chronically infected hosts can rise upon neutralization of cytokines (e.g. IFNγ or TNFα).
source: In chronically infected hosts, the pathogen population tends to diversify forming non-growing and growing subpopulations which are kept in check by immune defenses, but can rise upon neutralization of cytokines (e.g. IFNγ or TNFα) (Monack et al., 2004; Pham et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Monack et al., 2004; Pham et al., 2020.

claim: During monoclonal infections, intraspecies priority effects from S.Tm colonizing a given site within the host reduce the chances of colonization by pathogen cells that are arriving later.
source: During monoclonal infections characteristic of many experimental models, intraspecies priority effects from S.Tm colonizing a given site within the host reduce the chances of colonization by pathogen cells that are arriving later (Lam and Monack, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lam and Monack, 2014.

claim: Gut colonization is rarely a monoclonal process.
source: However, gut colonization is rarely a monoclonal process.
evidence: This is a statement based on knowledge and inference from the literature.

claim: Examples of multiple Enterobacteriaceae strains co-occuring in the same host have been demonstrated in longitudinal clinical studies monitoring fecal Enterobacteriaceae populations.
source: Examples of multiple Enterobacteriaceae strains co-occuring in the same host have been demonstrated in longitudinal clinical studies monitoring fecal Enterobacteriaceae populations, but also shown in swine where different strains of Salmonella colonize the lymph nodes compared to the gut lumen (León-Sampedro et al., 2021; Martinson et al., 2019; San Román et al., 2018; Tenaillon et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to León-Sampedro et al., 2021; Martinson et al., 2019; San Román et al., 2018; Tenaillon et al., 2010.

claim: In swine, different strains of Salmonella colonize the lymph nodes compared to the gut lumen.
source: Examples of multiple Enterobacteriaceae strains co-occuring in the same host have been demonstrated in longitudinal clinical studies monitoring fecal Enterobacteriaceae populations, but also shown in swine where different strains of Salmonella colonize the lymph nodes compared to the gut lumen (León-Sampedro et al., 2021; Martinson et al., 2019; San Román et al., 2018; Tenaillon et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to León-Sampedro et al., 2021; Martinson et al., 2019; San Román et al., 2018; Tenaillon et al., 2010.

claim: Repeated re-seeding and re-invasion events during persistent infection may promote plasmid spread.
source: Based on these considerations, we hypothesized that repeated re-seeding and re-invasion events during persistent infection may promote plasmid spread.
evidence: This is the hypothesis being tested in the study.

claim: Certain resistance plasmids should expedite re-seeding-transfer-invasion cycles within the infected host.
source: Finally, we reasoned that certain resistance plasmids should themselves expedite re-seeding-transfer-invasion cycles within the infected host.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on reasoning about plasmid-encoded resistance mechanisms.

claim: Plasmid-encoded resistance genes encoding enzymes degrading antibiotics with an extra-cytoplasmic target (e.g. beta-lactamases) should expedite re-seeding-transfer-invasion cycles.
source: In particular, this should pertain to plasmid-encoded resistance genes encoding enzymes degrading antibiotics with an extra-cytoplasmic target (e.g. beta-lactamases).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the mechanism of action of beta-lactamases.

claim: Extended spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBL) are capable of hydrolyzing a wide variety of beta-lactam antibiotics including ampicillin and cephalosporins.
source: Extended spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBL) capable of hydrolyzing a wide variety of beta-lactam antibiotics including ampicillin and cephalosporins are of particular concern, as beta-lactam antibiotics account for about two-thirds of the antibiotics deployed annually worldwide (World Health Organization, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2017.

claim: Beta-lactam antibiotics account for about two-thirds of the antibiotics deployed annually worldwide.
source: Extended spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBL) capable of hydrolyzing a wide variety of beta-lactam antibiotics including ampicillin and cephalosporins are of particular concern, as beta-lactam antibiotics account for about two-thirds of the antibiotics deployed annually worldwide (World Health Organization, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2017.

claim: Resistance plasmids encoding beta-lactamases are able to reach high density under beta-lactam treatment and clear the local environment from antibiotics, as shown in vitro.
source: These periplasmic enzymes may facilitate re-seeding of sensitive recipients, as resistance plasmids encoding beta-lactamases are able to reach high density under beta-lactam treatment, and clear the local environment from antibiotics, as shown in vitro (Perlin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Perlin et al., 2009.

claim: It had remained unclear if donor-mediated reduction of local beta-lactam concentrations would suffice for promoting survival of susceptible recipients in vivo prior to this study.
source: However, it had remained unclear if such donor-mediated reduction of local beta-lactam concentrations would suffice for promoting survival of susceptible recipients in vivo, fostering plasmid transfer and subsequent reservoir formation in the host's tissue.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: The study quantitatively assessed the link between within-host plasmid transfer, invasion-reservoir formation-re-seeding cycles and plasmid accumulation in the host's tissues using S.Tm mouse models.
source: To address this, we quantitatively assessed the link between within-host plasmid transfer, invasion-reservoir formation-re-seeding cycles and plasmid accumulation in the host's tissues using S.Tm mouse models for both antibiotic persistence and chronic infection.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach of the study.

claim: The study used donor-recipient-plasmid combinations featuring a high conjugation efficiency.
source: To study these processes in a proof-of-concept approach, we chose donor-recipient-plasmid combinations featuring a high conjugation efficiency and relieved potential restrictions to conjugation or reservoir formation in the mouse gut-like colonization resistance conferred by the microbiota, and priority effects of strains that already colonize tissue reservoirs.
evidence: This describes the experimental design choices.

claim: The study relieved potential restrictions to conjugation or reservoir formation like colonization resistance conferred by the microbiota.
source: To study these processes in a proof-of-concept approach, we chose donor-recipient-plasmid combinations featuring a high conjugation efficiency and relieved potential restrictions to conjugation or reservoir formation in the mouse gut-like colonization resistance conferred by the microbiota, and priority effects of strains that already colonize tissue reservoirs.
evidence: This describes the experimental design choices.

claim: The study relieved potential restrictions to conjugation or reservoir formation like priority effects of strains that already colonize tissue reservoirs.
source: To study these processes in a proof-of-concept approach, we chose donor-recipient-plasmid combinations featuring a high conjugation efficiency and relieved potential restrictions to conjugation or reservoir formation in the mouse gut-like colonization resistance conferred by the microbiota, and priority effects of strains that already colonize tissue reservoirs.
evidence: This describes the experimental design choices.

claim: The study demonstrated expansion of the plasmid diversity in the gut tissue reservoir.
source: Thereby, we could demonstrate expansion of the plasmid diversity in the gut tissue reservoir, a role for the chronically infecting S.Tm subpopulation and the effect of gut luminal antibiotic degradation by beta-lactamase expressing donor strains.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The study demonstrated a role for the chronically infecting S.Tm subpopulation in plasmid spread.
source: Thereby, we could demonstrate expansion of the plasmid diversity in the gut tissue reservoir, a role for the chronically infecting S.Tm subpopulation and the effect of gut luminal antibiotic degradation by beta-lactamase expressing donor strains.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The study demonstrated the effect of gut luminal antibiotic degradation by beta-lactamase expressing donor strains on plasmid spread.
source: Thereby, we could demonstrate expansion of the plasmid diversity in the gut tissue reservoir, a role for the chronically infecting S.Tm subpopulation and the effect of gut luminal antibiotic degradation by beta-lactamase expressing donor strains.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The i.p. infection model allows study of plasmid transfer in models for both antibiotic persistence and persistent infection.
source: The advantage of this i.p. infection model is threefold. First, it allows us to study plasmid transfer and subsequent tissue storage in models for antibiotic persistence (the focus of Bakkeren et al., 2019) and to extend the work to persistent infection (this work).
evidence: This describes the rationale for the experimental model used.

claim: The i.p. infection model ensures that plasmid transfer observed is truly a result of plasmid conjugation into recipients entering from tissue reservoirs into the gut lumen.
source: Second, i.p. infection bypasses the need for gut colonization, ensuring that plasmid transfer observed later in the experiment is truly a result of plasmid conjugation into recipients entering from tissue reservoirs into the gut lumen.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the experimental model used.

claim: The i.p. infection model mimics tissue reservoirs that are established after systemic spread following gut colonization.
source: Third, the i.p. infection model mimics tissue reservoirs that are established after systemic spread following gut colonization (and therefore allows us to study the role of persistent infection in plasmid transfer dynamics) (Bakkeren et al., 2019; Lam and Monack, 2014; Monack et al., 2004; Stecher et al., 2006).
evidence: This describes the rationale for the experimental model used, supported by citations.

claim: The i.p. infection model eliminates the contribution of priority effects attributable to the inoculation route.
source: We would like to point out a caveat of this i.p. model, in that it eliminates the contribution of priority effects attributable to the inoculation route.
evidence: This is a limitation of the experimental model acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Sites that are normally occupied by invading S.Tm cells (e.g. the mLN) are less colonized after an i.p. infection compared to an oral infection.
source: As natural infections would occur via the oral colonization route, sites that are normally occupied by invading S.Tm cells (e.g. the mesenteric lymph node; mLN) are less colonized after an i.p. infection compared to an oral infection.
evidence: This is an inference about the differences between i.p. and oral infection routes.

claim: Invasion events from the gut luminal side are likely over-estimated in the i.p. infection model.
source: This means that invasion events from the gut luminal side later in the experiment are likely over-estimated in this model.
evidence: This is an inference about a limitation of the experimental model.

claim: The i.p. infection model provides an exquisitely sensitive system to ask if tissue re-invasion can in principle expand the plasmid reservoirs within a host.
source: On the other hand, this provides us with an exquisitely sensitive system to ask if tissue re-invasion can in principle expand the plasmid reservoirs within a host.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the experimental model despite its limitations.

claim: One day after the addition of donors, recipients started re-seeding into the gut lumen and transconjugants were detected in the feces.
source: One day after the addition of donors (SL1344Avir P2cat), recipients started re-seeding into the gut lumen and transconjugants were detected in the feces (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results.

claim: By day 10 of the experiment, transconjugants were detected in the majority of mice (8/13 mice) in the S.TmWT group.
source: By day 10 of the experiment, transconjugants were detected in the majority of mice (8/13 mice; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results.

claim: Plasmid transfer was confirmed by performing PCRs with both plasmid- and recipient-specific primers.
source: We confirmed that plasmid transfer had occurred by performing PCRs with both plasmid- and recipient-specific primers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes a validation experiment.

claim: Re-seeding and plasmid acquisition depended on the TTSS-2 encoded on SPI-2.
source: Re-seeding and plasmid acquisition depended on the TTSS-2 encoded on Salmonella pathogenicity island (SPI)-2, as recipients lacking a functional TTSS-2 (14028S ssaV mutant; S.TmSPI-2) failed to re-seed frequently, and consequently transconjugants were rarely observed (1/8 mice; Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results showing the role of TTSS-2.

claim: The failure of S.TmSPI-2 to establish substantial tissue reservoir sizes could explain the limited re-seeding.
source: Their failure to establish substantial tissue reservoir sizes (e.g. in the spleen, liver, or gall bladder) could explain the limited re-seeding of S.TmSPI-2 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations.

claim: Re-seeding was not dependent on the TTSS-1 encoded on SPI-1.
source: However, re-seeding was not dependent on the TTSS-1 encoded on SPI-1, as mutant recipient strains that lack a functional TTSS-1 apparatus (14028S invG mutant; S.TmSPI-1) established tissue reservoirs and re-seeded the gut (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results showing TTSS-1 is not required.

claim: The presence of donors did not promote re-seeding of recipients.
source: Re-seeding was detected in both groups (2/4 mice with donors; 3/5 mice without donors by day 10 of the experiment), indicating that the presence of donors did not promote re-seeding (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a description of control experiment results.

claim: Bacteria re-seeding from tissue reservoirs can gain plasmids in the gut.
source: Altogether, these results indicated that bacteria re-seeding from tissue reservoirs can gain plasmids in the gut.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Tissue reservoir-promoted plasmid transfer dynamics can happen during persistent infection involving phenotypically susceptible pathogen cells.
source: Most likely, tissue reservoir-promoted plasmid transfer dynamics will happen during persistent infection involving phenotypically susceptible pathogen cells, provided multiple strains co-occur within a host.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental results.

claim: An overarching re-seeding-conjugation-re-invasion cycle could result in the distribution of different alleles in the various strains colonizing a host.
source: Since a natural ecological succession of Enterobacteriaceae has been documented in the gut (León-Sampedro et al., 2021; Martinson et al., 2019), an overarching re-seeding-conjugation-re-invasion cycle could result in the distribution of different alleles in the various strains colonizing a host.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental results and cited literature.

claim: Host tissue reservoirs would dramatically expand the time scale of horizontal gene transfer.
source: The host tissue reservoirs would dramatically expand the time scale of such transfer thereby enabling horizontal gene transfer even when the initial donor and the later recipient have never 'co-existed' within the host.
evidence: This is a speculation about the implications of the findings.

claim: Different strains of commensal and pathogenic Enterobacteriaceae that show vastly different plasmid, prophage, and mutational profiles are often observed within a given host population or even within the same host.
source: In line with this hypothesis, different strains of commensal and pathogenic Enterobacteriaceae that show vastly different plasmid, prophage, and mutational profiles are often observed within a given host population or even within the same host (Desai et al., 2013; Kroger et al., 2012; Martinson et al., 2019; San Román et al., 2018; Tenaillon et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The same plasmid has been detected in different enterobacterial strains over time within the same patient.
source: Conversely, the same plasmid has been detected in different enterobacterial strains over time within the same patient (León-Sampedro et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to León-Sampedro et al., 2021.

claim: The role of the pathogen's re-seeding-acquisition-re-invasion cycles in resistance plasmid transfer may be particularly important in cases where different S.Tm are present within the same host.
source: The role of the pathogen's re-seeding-acquisition-re-invasion cycles in resistance plasmid transfer may be particularly important in cases where different S.Tm are present within the same host (e.g. the gut lumen vs. the host tissues), as observed in pig farms (San Román et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to San Román et al., 2018.

claim: Re-seeding of recipient strains from tissue reservoirs is the rate-limiting step for the formation of new transconjugant reservoirs.
source: Through population dynamic analysis, we showed that re-seeding of recipient strains from tissue reservoirs is the rate-limiting step for the formation of new transconjugant reservoirs (Figure 2; Figure 5, step 2a).
evidence: This is a conclusion from mathematical modeling and experimental data.

claim: The gall bladder may not be the primary route of re-seeding in the i.p. infection model.
source: The gall bladder contained some S.Tm, but the low densities suggest that the gall bladder is not the primary route of re-seeding in this model (as suggested in some other experimental models Lam and Monack, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations and comparison to cited literature.

claim: Sequence tags in the gall bladder did not necessarily correlate with those found at highest density in the feces.
source: In our experimental model, we found that sequence tags in the gall bladder did not necessarily correlate with those found at highest density in the feces, suggesting, along with others (Lam and Monack, 2014), that additional routes of re-seeding may exist.
evidence: This is a description of experimental results.

claim: Phagocytic cells such as macrophages and dendritic cells serve as reservoirs for S.Tm.
source: Phagocytic cells such as macrophages and dendritic cells serve as reservoirs for S.Tm (Claudi et al., 2014; Helaine et al., 2014; Kaiser et al., 2014; Pham et al., 2020; Rosenberg et al., 2021; Stapels et al., 2018) and can be reactivated by IFNγ depletion (Monack et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The high density of S.Tm in the tissues that line S.I. GALT, correlating with S.Tm found in the gut lumen of the small intestine, could suggest that trafficking of S.Tm-bearing immune cells to these sites contributes to gut luminal re-seeding.
source: The high density of S.Tm in the tissues that line S.I. GALT, correlating with S.Tm found in the gut lumen of the small intestine, could suggest that trafficking of S.Tm-bearing immune cells to these sites (Habtezion et al., 2016) contributes to gut luminal re-seeding.
evidence: This is a speculation based on experimental observations and cited literature.

claim: The independence of S.Tm on its TTSS-1 for re-seeding appears to support host-mediated trafficking to the gut lumen rather than an active mechanism evolved by S.Tm.
source: The independence of S.Tm on its TTSS-1 for re-seeding appears to support host-mediated trafficking to the gut lumen rather than an active mechanism evolved by S.Tm, but further work is needed for confirmation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on experimental observations.

claim: Vaccination has shown success in reducing the formation of tissue reservoirs and consequently plasmid transfer dynamics associated with re-seeding.
source: Interventions such as vaccination have shown success in reducing the formation of tissue reservoirs and consequently plasmid transfer dynamics associated with re-seeding (Bakkeren et al., 2019; Moor et al., 2017; Moor et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Once re-seeding occurred, the transfer of plasmids followed by re-invasion is likely, given a sufficiently high carrying capacity in the gut lumen.
source: Here, we showed that once re-seeding occurred, the transfer of plasmids followed by re-invasion is likely, given a sufficiently high carrying capacity (as a proxy for decreased colonization resistance) in the gut lumen.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data and modeling.

claim: Plasmid transfer is dependent on both the density of donors and recipients.
source: This is because plasmid transfer is dependent on both the density of donors and recipients.
evidence: This is established knowledge about conjugation dynamics.

claim: Invasion may be density-dependent.
source: Invasion may also be density-dependent (Ackermann et al., 2008); approximately 300 invasion events occur into the mLN per day initially in streptomycin-pretreated mouse models (Kaiser et al., 2013) and this likely decreases proportionally with colonization.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ackermann et al., 2008 and Kaiser et al., 2013.

claim: In a healthy microbiota community, colonization resistance prohibits enterobacteriaceal blooms in >90% of the hosts.
source: In a healthy microbiota community, colonization resistance prohibits enterobacteriaceal blooms in >90% of the hosts (Stecher et al., 2010; Stecher and Hardt, 2011) and dramatically reduces the efficiency of plasmid transfer (Stecher et al., 2012; Wotzka et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stecher et al., 2010; Stecher and Hardt, 2011; Stecher et al., 2012; Wotzka et al., 2019.

claim: Gut perturbations such as diet shifts, inflammation, antibiotic treatment, or a reduction in microbiota complexity can all lead to increases in loads of Enterobacteriaceae and consequently plasmid transfer.
source: However, gut perturbations such as diet shifts, inflammation, antibiotic treatment, or a reduction in microbiota complexity (e.g. dysbiosis) can all lead to increases in loads of Enterobacteriaceae and consequently plasmid transfer (Figure 5, step 3) (Bakkeren et al., 2019; Barthel et al., 2003; Benz et al., 2021; Kreuzer and Hardt, 2020; Stecher et al., 2012; Stecher et al., 2007; Wotzka et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: A healthy microbiota is integral in minimizing pathogen evolution by reducing horizontal gene transfer and by reducing the likelihood of re-invasion and subsequent formation of tissue reservoirs.
source: Therefore, a healthy microbiota is integral in minimizing pathogen evolution in two complementary ways, by reducing horizontal gene transfer and by reducing the likelihood of re-invasion and subsequent formation of tissue reservoirs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and cited literature.

claim: Plasmids encoding secreted antibiotic degrading enzymes can promote their own spread by protecting potential new recipients sensitive to the antibiotic.
source: Lastly, we showed that plasmids encoding secreted antibiotic degrading enzymes can promote their own spread by an additional mechanism in vivo: protecting potential new recipients sensitive to the antibiotic (Figure 5, step 2b).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Re-seeding of S.Tm, initially susceptible to the beta-lactam, can occur even during beta-lactam therapy, dependent on the presence of E. coli-producing beta-lactamase.
source: Re-seeding of S.Tm, initially susceptible to the beta-lactam, can occur even during beta-lactam therapy, dependent on the presence of E. coli-producing beta-lactamase (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results.

claim: The prevalence of ESBL-producing E. coli is rising in recent years.
source: The prevalence of ESBL-producing E. coli is rising in recent years, and ESBL genes are frequently plasmid-encoded (Temkin et al., 2014; World Health Organization, 2017; Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Temkin et al., 2014; World Health Organization, 2017; Yang et al., 2009.

claim: ESBL genes are frequently plasmid-encoded.
source: The prevalence of ESBL-producing E. coli is rising in recent years, and ESBL genes are frequently plasmid-encoded (Temkin et al., 2014; World Health Organization, 2017; Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Temkin et al., 2014; World Health Organization, 2017; Yang et al., 2009.

claim: Beta-lactamases are public goods.
source: The extracellularly acting beta-lactamases are therefore public goods.
evidence: This is a statement based on the mechanism of action of beta-lactamases.

claim: Beta-lactamases allow the survival of susceptible S.Tm in the presence of otherwise lethal concentrations of ampicillin in vitro.
source: In vitro this was shown to allow the survival of susceptible S.Tm in the presence of otherwise lethal concentrations of ampicillin (Perlin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Perlin et al., 2009.

claim: The same process of beta-lactamase-mediated protection occurs in the gut lumen, with re-seeding S.Tm followed by conjugation, clonal expansion, and tissue re-invasion as a consequence.
source: In our experiments, we showed that the same process occurs in the gut lumen, with re-seeding S.Tm followed by conjugation, clonal expansion, and tissue re-invasion as a consequence (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results.

claim: Antibiotic treatment could serve to amplify re-seeding followed by plasmid exchange and tissue reservoir reformation, given sufficient protection from the antibiotic in trans.
source: As one of the prodigal mechanisms for blooms (of resistant bacteria), antibiotic treatment could serve to amplify re-seeding followed by plasmid exchange and tissue reservoir reformation, given sufficient protection from the antibiotic in trans.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental results.

claim: Many antibiotic resistance genes encode antibiotic-inactivating enzymes, even if they are not secreted.
source: Many antibiotic resistance genes encode antibiotic-inactivating enzymes, even if they are not secreted (D'Costa et al., 2006), as is the case of beta-lactamases.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to D'Costa et al., 2006.

claim: The transient overexpression of efflux pumps was shown to confer survival long enough to obtain a plasmid in the presence of tetracycline above the MIC in vitro.
source: The transient overexpression of efflux pumps was shown to confer survival long enough to obtain a plasmid in the presence of tetracycline above the MIC in vitro (Nolivos et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nolivos et al., 2019.

claim: Bacterial strains that produce outer membrane vesicles have been shown to lead to an altered susceptibility to antimicrobial peptides.
source: Moreover, bacterial strains that produce outer membrane vesicles have been shown to lead to an altered susceptibility to antimicrobial peptides (e.g. polymyxin B or colistin, shown in several bacteria including E. coli and Salmonella Typhi) (Manning and Kuehn, 2011; Marchant et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Manning and Kuehn, 2011; Marchant et al., 2021.

claim: Polymyxin resistance could be functionally transferred to sensitive bacteria mediated by outer membrane vesicles.
source: One study found that polymyxin resistance could even be functionally transferred to sensitive bacteria mediated by outer membrane vesicles (Marchant et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Marchant et al., 2021.

claim: Plasmids can subvert tissue-associated pathogen reservoirs to promote long-term carriage within the host and subsequent spread.
source: Overall, here we show that plasmids can subvert tissue-associated pathogen reservoirs to promote long-term carriage within the host and subsequent spread.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study.

claim: There are two types of tissue reservoirs with partially complementary features: those formed by enteropathogens in chronic infections and those formed by persistent pathogen cells.
source: There seem to be two types of tissue reservoirs with partially complementary features (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Tissue-associated reservoirs formed by enteropathogens in chronic infections are relatively large and facilitate re-seeding of the gut lumen and subsequent plasmid transfer at relatively high rates.
source: The tissue-associated reservoirs formed by enteropathogens in chronic (persistent) infections are relatively large and facilitate re-seeding of the gut lumen and subsequent plasmid transfer at relatively high rates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Persistent pathogen cells are less frequent and need to re-start growth before engaging in any luminal plasmid transfers, likely making them less efficient at luminal re-seeding.
source: In contrast, persistent pathogen cells are less frequent and need to re-start growth before engaging in any luminal plasmid transfers, likely making them less efficient at luminal re-seeding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and comparison to previous work.

claim: Persistent pathogen cells ensure survival of recipients and plasmid reservoir maintenance even in cases of therapy with antibiotics to which these persisters are genetically susceptible.
source: However, they ensure survival of recipients and plasmid reservoir maintenance even in cases of therapy with antibiotics to which these persisters are genetically susceptible.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and previous work.

claim: The study provides a proof-of-concept that tissue reservoirs can act as a record of evolutionary events such as plasmid transfer in the gut lumen.
source: Our study provides a proof-of-concept that tissue reservoirs can act as a record of evolutionary events such as plasmid transfer in the gut lumen.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study.

claim: It is conceivable that mutational events or transfer of other mobile genetic elements, for example, bacteriophages carrying accessory genes, could also be stored in tissue reservoirs.
source: It is conceivable that mutational events or transfer of other mobile genetic elements, for example, bacteriophages carrying accessory genes, could also be stored in tissue reservoirs.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential extensions of the findings.
